To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we propose DriPP, a new statistical model for event-related potentials (ERPs) and neural oscillations, (2) we develop a novel expectation-maximization algorithm, (3) we show that DriPP is able to identify neural responses and to separate them from non-task specific events, and (4) we demonstrate that DriPP provides an efficient alternative to the standard ERP analysis
we propose a novel statistical point-process model for the analysis of M/EEG signals.
we develop a new statistical model to analyze M/EEG data in an unsupervized fashion, which is able to detect and characterize task-related patterns and non-task-related patterns.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the statistical analysis of neural signals and provides new tools for the quantitative analysis of M/EEG data.
the analysis of event-based descriptions of MEG data, and we provide a novel point process approach that is able to model the effect of stimuli on neural responses.
the development of novel statistical methods to analyze electrophysiological data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DriPP model is a promising tool for the analysis of MEG/EEG data.
DriPP is a novel point process model to analyze MEG/EEG signals and that DriPP can be used to detect and model neural responses to external stimuli.
DriPP is an efficient method for modeling and detecting patterns in M/EEGs, which is based on a principled statistical framework.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose an unsupervised methodology that allows to model the effect of a cognitive manipulation on the temporal dynamics of the brain.
we develop a new methodology to model and extract neural responses in a principled way from MEG/EEG data.
we develop a principled statistical framework to model and estimate the effect of stimuli on neural signals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
point process models are a natural and efficient framework to study the effect of cognitive tasks or experimental manipulations on brain activity.
DriPP can be used to identify the effect of experimental manipulations on neural responses in a principled way.
point processes can be used to analyze event-based representations of electrophysiology data, and that they can be used to model the impact of cognitive manipulations.
